The anion exchange reactions were carried out in the dark and under a N₂ atmosphere to prevent potential decomposition of the silver salts.  These reactions occurred over different time periods, depending on the silver salt used.  While the reaction with silver triflate went to completion in just a few hours, the reaction with silver lactate took days.  Products 2 and 3 were isolated from the reaction mixture by filtering out the silver salt and evaporating the solvent.  Their ¹H NMR spectra in the relatively non-polar CDCl₃ solvent show quite distinctive resonances for the chiral CH(OH) groups.  Compound 3—with the lactate anion—exhibits the biggest chemical shift differences between the methine and hydroxyl protons (1.9 ppm), consistent with the expectation that the lactate anion can most readily form hydrogen bonds to the hydroxyl group.  Compound 2 also has a relatively large differences between the methine and hydroxyl chemical shifts (0.6 ppm) compared to that in the parent compound 1 (0.1 ppm), suggesting a degree of hydrogen bonding to the hydroxyl proton that is intermediate between that in 3 and 1.
Attempted alkylation at the hydroxyl group

The hydroxyl group in hydroquinine is located at a chiral center and its modification into an ether group can potentially lead to new CILs with variable chiral environments, depending on the ether substituents.  To this end, we hypothesized that deprotonation of the hydroxyl group on hydroquinine may generate an alkoxide that can compete effectively with the more bulky tertiary nitrogen center of the quinuclidine moiety in an SN2 reaction with an alkyl halide such as dibromobutane (Scheme 3).  Subsequent intramolecular reaction of the remaining bromide functionality with either the quinuclidine nitrogen or an external N-butyl imidiazolium bromide would yield ether-modified hydroquinines that could be used as the cationic components in CILs.  Unfortunately, neither of these reaction sequences proceeded to completion in our hands, and we were unable to isolate a single major product after numerous tries.  Monitoring the reaction using TLC reveals several reaction byproducts that could arise from either competitive reaction of the alkyl halide with the quinuclidine or dimerization through the dibromobutane linkage.  Although unverified, it is also possible that elimination products also formed.  Attempts to separate the reaction mixture using chromatography

Melting points

Modifying the quinuclidine nitrogen with different substituents and exchanging the resulting cations with different anions afforded compounds with a wide range of melting points.  Table 1 shows that compound 4 has a lower melting point than the similar compound 1, probably due to the larger steric size of the iodide anion and the longer tail on the quaternary ammonium center. The degree of hydrogen bonding and the surface-area-to-charge ratio can be used to explain the melting points in the homologous series 1-3.  Compound 3, with the best hydrogen-bonding potential and the largest surface-area-to-charge ratio for the anion has the lowest melting point. By the same argument, compound 1 should have the highest melting point, which is indeed observed.

It is important to note that not all of the compounds synthesized here are ILs in the strictest definition of the term.  Because some (1, 2) melt above 100°C, they can only be considered as “proto-CILs”, compounds that can serve as the building blocks from which different CILs can be synthesized by further anion exchange or covalent modification to the hydroquinine cation. Conclusion and Future Work

We reported the successful syntheses of several CILs and proto-CILs from hydroquinine via amine quarternization and anion exchange reactions.  To the best of our knowledge, our work constituted the first attempt to systematically modify the hydroquinine framework for potential use in CILs.  Even though some of our compounds melt above 100°C and thus are not strictly ILs, they can be readily converted into ILs with a different anion.

We also attempted to modify the hydroxyl group at the chiral center of hydroquinine, which would expand the variety of cations that could be made from this natural precursor.  Unfortunately, our efforts did not reliably produce a single identifiable product.  Further work can be devoted to developing reaction conditions that will allow for selective and complete modification of this functional group.  In addition, our CILs should be tested with several catalytic systems to assess their potential as asymmetry-inducing solvents.
Experimental

All reactions were conducted under ambient laboratory conditions unless otherwise noted.  For anhydrous syntheses, HPLC-grade toluene, methylene chloride, and chloroform were obtained from Fisher Scientific and dried over neutral alumina via the Dow-Grubbs solvent system installed by Glass Contours (Laguna Beach, CA).¹²  The solvents were collected under argon, degassed under vacuum, and stored under nitrogen in Straus flasks prior to use.  For bench-top syntheses, HPLC-grade toluene was obtained from Aldrich and used without further purifications.  Deuterated solvents (Aldrich Chemicals and Cambridge Isotope Laboratories) and n-butyl bromide (Avocado Organics) were purchased from commercial sources and used as received.  All other reagents were purchased from Aldrich Chemicals and used without further purification.
